headline: Netflix paid $587M for Ben Affleck's AI filmmaking startup
summary: The streaming giant acquired InterPositive, co-founded by Affleck, for its AI tools that enhance footage in post-production.
details: Netflix has officially revealed the acquisition of InterPositive, a startup co-founded by actor and director Ben Affleck, for $587 million in cash.
The AI-powered startup's tools are designed to assist filmmakers in post-production, addressing challenges like missing shots, incorrect lighting, and background replacements.
Affleck stated his goal was to 'protect the power of human creativity' through the acquisition, with the entire InterPositive team joining Netflix.

While Netflix announced the acquisition in March, the financial terms were not disclosed until a recent regulatory filing. A Bloomberg report had previously estimated the deal value at up to $600 million.
This move aligns with Netflix's increasing integration of generative AI, with approximately 300 of its titles already utilizing the technology.

headline_marked: [[AI advice]] makes users 3x less accurate, 2x more confident, study finds
headline: AI advice makes users 3x less accurate, 2x more confident, study finds
summary: Researchers found that relying on AI tools significantly decreased accuracy and suppressed the ability to admit ignorance, while boosting user confidence.
details: A new study reveals a concerning trend: the availability of AI advice drastically reduces human accuracy and critical thinking. Researchers observed that people's willingness to admit they don't know dropped from 44% to just 3% when using AI tools.
Accuracy plummeted from 27% to 9% in tasks where AI was consulted. Simultaneously, confidence in their answers surged from 30% to a striking 76%, even when the AI provided incorrect information.

The study intentionally used questions where AI models typically fail, such as recalling visual details from films. This ensured that any decrease in judgment couldn't be attributed to users sensibly delegating to a reliable tool.
Even with monetary incentives, the effect persisted, with accuracy only rising to 16% and admitting ignorance to 8%—still far below baseline levels without AI.
This phenomenon, dubbed 'cognitive surrender' by some researchers, highlights that the mere presence of AI can suppress the crucial cognitive habit of recognizing the limits of one's own knowledge.
Experts are particularly concerned about children developing critical thinking skills in an era where AI products are designed to always provide answers, potentially teaching users to do the same.
caption:
AI makes you dumber and more confident about it, new research shows. The ability to say 'I don't know' is vanishing.

A new study reveals a concerning trend: the availability of AI advice drastically reduces human accuracy and critical thinking. Researchers observed that people's willingness to admit they don't know dropped from 44% to just 3% when using AI tools.

Accuracy plummeted from 27% to 9% in tasks where AI was consulted. Simultaneously, confidence in their answers surged from 30% to a striking 76%, even when the AI provided incorrect information.

The study intentionally used questions where AI models typically fail, such as recalling visual details from films. This ensured that any decrease in judgment couldn't be attributed to users sensibly delegating to a reliable tool.

Even with monetary incentives, the effect persisted, with accuracy only rising to 16% and admitting ignorance to 8%—still far below baseline levels without AI.

This phenomenon, dubbed 'cognitive surrender' by some researchers, highlights that the mere presence of AI can suppress the crucial cognitive habit of recognizing the limits of one's own knowledge.

Experts are particularly concerned about children developing critical thinking skills in an era where AI products are designed to always provide answers, potentially teaching users to do the same.
